sentences.text: Dahalokely was a meat-eating theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Madagascar, earning the name "small thief" because it measured only 3.5 meters in length.
Its species name, tokana, translates to "lonely" or "solitary," a reference to the isolation of the Malagasy landmass.
The known remains include a partial skeleton of a young individual that preserves vertebrae and ribs but lacks a skull.
It was initially thought to be 3.5 meters long based on the assumption that it shared the typical build of other abelisaurids.
However, if the animal possessed the elongated body shape seen in noasaurids, its length would have ranged from 4.2 to 5.6 meters.
Joseph Sertich first found the remains of a new theropod near Antsiranana in 2007 during an expedition led by Andrew Farke.
These specimens were recovered from the Ambolafotsy Formation in northern Madagascar, dating to approximately 93 million years ago.
The neck vertebrae show a markedly convex lamina between the prezygapophysis and epipophysis, a feature longer than the vertebral body and separated by notches.
Additionally, the second dorsal vertebra possesses strongly concave joint facets on its rear processes.
When first described in 2013, the genus was placed in the superfamily Abelisauroidea, but by 2014 it was classified as a basal noasaurid.
Its vertebrae and ribs display traits found in both Noasauridae and Abelisauridae, yet an initial analysis placing it as a basal Noasaurid received weak support.
The incomplete nature of the fossils and the lack of comparable material make it difficult to determine its precise relationships with other abelisauroid members.
Dahalokely lived during the Turonian stage, between 93.9 and 89.8 million years ago, in the middle of the Cretaceous period.
At this time, Madagascar and India formed a single landmass called Indo-Madagascar that had separated from the rest of Gondwana.
This dinosaur is the only known species from Madagascar that lived when the island was still connected to India.
A 2018 study recovered Dahalokely within the subfamily Majungasaurinae alongside the Indian abelisaurid Rahiolisaurus, while a 2021 study placed both as basal brachyrostran carnotaurines.
Separate studies from 2018 and 2022, however, recovered the animal as a noasaurid based on phylogenetic analyses.
